newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy telecom delay may hurt credibility-Van Miert.
newsitem.headline: Italy telecom delay may hurt credibility-Van Miert.

text.p: Delays by the Italian government in preparing Italy's telecommunications industry for full-scale liberalisation on January 1 1998 could hurt Italy's credibility, EU Commissioner Karel Van Miert was quoted as saying.

Van Miert told Milan daily Corriere della Sera that he was particularly concerned over the failure of the government to win parliamentary approval for the establishment of an authority to regulate the industry.

"We have serious worries and note that in the majority of other countries legislation has already been passed to create the national authority on telecommunications and to fix the rules of the game with a view to total liberalisation on January 1, 1998," said Van Miert.
"In Italy, with all the time that has been wasted, I wonder how they will manage to make it," said Van Miert.
Van Miert said that many of the delays were due to difficulties encountered by the government in getting its legislative programme through parliament.

"I have to note that with regard to commitments made not only with the European Union but also the WTO (World Trade Organisation), there is a risk of delays and complications. It will not be a good thing for Italy's credibility," he said.
Van Miert also said he had received confirmation in writing from the government that Telecom Italia Mobile would make a 60 billion lire indemnity payment to its rival Omnitel.

The payment is compensation for the licence fee that it was forced to pay when it started up its mobile phone service in 1995 in competition with TIM, which until then had enjoyed a monopoly in mobile telephony.
Van Miert said he was concerned that the allocation of new GSM frequencies, currently assigned to the armed forces, could give rise to further distorsion of competition.
"Here there is a risk of a further complication because TIM now occupies frequencies which should be available also for the second operator (Omnitel)," he said.

"If in order to buy the new frequencies made available by the military only the second operator is forced to pay there is a risk of creating a new element of distorsion of competition," he added. --Milan newsroom +392-66102321
